content: Ketoprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and antirheumatic properties. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, pain, and dysmenorrhea. However, its use is associated with significant risks, including cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, renal, and hypersensitivity reactions, which require careful consideration and monitoring. Black Box Warning Clinical trials have demonstrated an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, with NSAID use. These events can be fatal and may occur without prior symptoms. Patients with existing cardiovascular disease or risk factors are at greater risk. To minimize these risks, the lowest effective dose should be used for the shortest duration possible. NSAIDs, including ketoprofen, are contraindicated for perioperative pain management in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Adult Dosage For adults, the recommended oral dosage is 75 mg every 8 hours or 50 mg every 6 hours, with a maximum daily dose of 300 mg. Higher doses do not provide additional analgesic benefits and may increase the risk of adverse effects. Off-label use for episodic migraine prevention has limited evidence. Pediatric Use Ketoprofen is not FDA-approved for use in patients under 18 years of age. Limited information exists regarding off-label use in pediatric populations. Contraindications Ketoprofen should not be administered to patients with a history of asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions to aspirin or other NSAIDs. It is also contraindicated in patients undergoing CABG surgery. Cardiovascular Effects NSAIDs, including ketoprofen, may cause new-onset hypertension or worsen preexisting hypertension, contributing to an increased risk of cardiovascular events. Blood pressure should be closely monitored during treatment. Fluid retention and edema have been observed in some patients, necessitating caution in those with heart failure or fluid retention. Gastrointestinal Effects Ketoprofen can cause serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events, including inflammation, bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These events may occur at any time, with or without warning symptoms. Patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding are at significantly higher risk. Concomitant use of corticosteroids, anticoagulants, smoking, alcohol consumption, older age, and poor general health further increase the risk. To reduce the likelihood of GI complications, the lowest effective dose should be used for the shortest duration, and patients should be monitored for signs of GI bleeding. Renal Effects Long-term NSAID use has been associated with renal papillary necrosis and other renal injuries. Patients with impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, or those taking diuretics or ACE inhibitors are at greater risk of renal decompensation. Ketoprofen is not recommended for patients with advanced renal disease. If treatment is necessary, renal function should be closely monitored. Hypersensitivity Reactions Anaphylactoid reactions may occur without prior exposure to ketoprofen. Patients with the aspirin triad (asthma, rhinitis, and nasal polyps) are at increased risk of severe bronchospasm and should not receive ketoprofen. Emergency medical attention is required for anaphylactoid reactions. Skin Reactions Serious skin adverse events, including exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), have been reported and may be fatal. Patients should discontinue ketoprofen at the first sign of skin rash or hypersensitivity. Pregnancy and Lactation Ketoprofen should be avoided in late pregnancy due to the risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus. Its effects on labor and delivery are unknown. It is not recommended for use in nursing mothers, as its excretion in human milk is not well studied. Geriatric Use Elderly patients are at increased risk of adverse effects, including GI bleeding and renal impairment. Ketoprofen clearance is reduced in older patients, necessitating dose adjustments and careful monitoring of renal function. Initial dosages should be reduced for patients over 75 years of age. Adverse Reactions Common adverse reactions include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, flatulence, headache, dizziness, and somnolence. Less common but serious reactions include GI bleeding, renal impairment, hepatic dysfunction, and hypersensitivity reactions. Drug Interactions Ketoprofen may interact with other medications, including ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium, methotrexate, and warfarin. These interactions can increase the risk of adverse effects, such as renal failure, elevated plasma drug levels, and GI bleeding. Concomitant use with aspirin is not recommended due to increased GI toxicity. Overdose Acute overdose symptoms include lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain. Severe cases may involve respiratory depression, coma, or convulsions. Management involves supportive care, gut decontamination with activated charcoal, and monitoring for complications. There is no specific antidote for ketoprofen overdose. Pharmacology Ketoprofen exerts its effects by inhibiting prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis, stabilizing lysosomal membranes, and exhibiting antibradykinin activity. It is highly protein-bound and has a half-life of 1.5 to 2 hours. Food slows its absorption but does not affect its overall bioavailability. Monitoring Patients on long-term ketoprofen therapy should undergo periodic complete blood counts (CBC) and liver function tests. Signs of GI bleeding, renal dysfunction, or hypersensitivity should prompt immediate evaluation and discontinuation of the drug if necessary. Administration Ketoprofen is available in immediate-release and extended-release formulations. Steady-state concentrations are achieved within 24 hours of initiating treatment. It should be administered with caution in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, and doses should be individualized based on patient response and tolerability.
